molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.activity_type_context: Genetic Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD), including autosomal dominant FTD caused by C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT mutations; Frontotemporal lobar degeneration with TDP-43 pathology (FTLD-TDP); FTLD-Tau pathology; Neuroaxonal degeneration; TDP-43 proteinopathies, tauopathies, and α-synucleinopathies related to TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele dosage.
molecular_mechanism_and_relationship.mechanism_description: The TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele is an alternate/protective allele that confers protection against FTLD-TDP by modifying the effects of FTD mutations (specifically GRN and C9orf72) on neurodegeneration (grey matter atrophy, NfL levels) and cognition (cognitive and behavioural measures). It exerts protective effects against neurodegeneration, leading to reduced grey matter atrophy and lower serum neurofilament light chain (NfL) levels, improving cognitive and behavioral functions, and reducing the risk of conversion to clinical FTD in mutation carriers. These protective effects appear to be additive based on G allele dosage, with no observed deviations from an additive effect for any phenotype. TMEM106B, a lysosomal integral membrane glycoprotein, is involved in cell debris clearance. Its dysfunction, such as upregulation of TMEM106B (associated with the risk A allele), leads to improper lysosomal formation, poor acidification, attenuated transport, and increased lysosomal stress. Conversely, double knock-out models of Tmem106b -/- and Grn -/- mice show exacerbated disease pathology and accumulation of phosphorylated TDP-43, suggesting the G allele protects by modulating lysosomal function and thereby influencing TDP-43 pathology. The presence of TMEM106B amyloid protein fibrils in human brains with various proteinopathies suggests a putative role for its pathological fibrillization across neurodegenerative diseases.
related_biomarkers: Risk of conversion to clinical FTD

dose_intensity_and_specificity.dose_comparison_summary: The study consistently found additive protective effects of the TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele, where increasing G allele dosage (0, 1, or 2 alleles) was associated with protective effects on various endophenotypes. No deviations from an additive effect were observed for any phenotype. While a recessive model (two G alleles for protection) was previously suggested for GRN-associated FTLD-TDP, this study's additive findings indicate that even one protective G allele confers benefit. For GRN carriers, the protective effect on grey matter atrophy was stronger in symptomatic carriers (0.013-0.02 ΔpGM per G allele/year) compared to presymptomatic carriers (0.004-0.006 ΔpGM per G allele/year). In survival analysis, the GRN-TMEM106B AG group showed a significantly lower risk of conversion (HR: 0.22) compared to GRN-TMEM106B AA, and the GG group had no converters, strongly indicating a dose-dependent protective effect.
dose_intensity_and_specificity.specificity_finding: The protective effects of TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele dosage are predominantly observed and highly specific to GRN and C9orf72 genetic FTD groups, which are associated with FTLD-TDP pathology. TMEM106B modifies FTLD-TDP pathology more strongly than FTLD-Tau pathology. In MAPT carriers (FTLD-Tau), minimal protective effects were noted (only reduced atrophy in the right inferior frontal gyrus in symptomatic carriers), with no effects on serum NfL or cognitive/behavioural measures. Specific effects were seen in C9orf72 carriers on baseline atrophy (presymptomatic), and longitudinally on atrophy, executive functions, language, global cognition, and behavior (symptomatic). For GRN carriers, effects were on longitudinal atrophy (presymptomatic and symptomatic), NfL (presymptomatic and symptomatic, baseline and longitudinal), global cognition (symptomatic baseline), and attention/processing speed (symptomatic longitudinal). No protective effects on memory were found in any gene group. The effects extend to other patient groups and healthy individuals but are most pronounced in GRN mutation carriers. GRN symptomatic cases often present with language impairment, while C9orf72 symptomatic cases show a higher prevalence of behavioral features, influencing the observed protective effects.

clinical_implication_and_population.target_population: Individuals with genetic Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD) caused by autosomal dominant mutations in C9orf72, GRN, or MAPT, including presymptomatic and symptomatic carriers, and non-carrier controls. This encompasses individuals at risk for FTLD-TDP and FTLD-Tau, as well as broader implications for healthy older adults and Parkinson’s disease patients.
clinical_implication_and_population.health_implication: The TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele confers a protective benefit against neurodegeneration and cognitive decline in individuals with genetic FTD, particularly those with GRN and C9orf72 mutations. It is associated with slower disease progression, reduced grey matter atrophy, lower serum NfL levels, better preservation of cognitive and behavioral functions, and a significantly lower risk of conversion to clinical FTD. This suggests a potential to slow disease progression and improve clinical prognosis, possibly leading to a longer asymptomatic period or later onset of symptoms. Conversely, the A allele is detrimental, associated with lower cortical volumes, greater cognitive decline (MMSE score), and influences age of onset in GRN carriers. Increased NfL levels in presymptomatic individuals may predict short-term risk of conversion to clinical FTD.
clinical_implication_and_population.risk_classification: Protective benefit (TMEM106B-rs1990622 G allele) against neurodegeneration and FTD progression; Adverse risk (TMEM106B-rs1990622 A allele) leading to lower cortical volumes and greater cognitive decline; Diagnostic utility (NfL for neuroaxonal degeneration and conversion risk); Prognostic marker/Disease course modifier for genetic FTD.

biomarker_reliability_and_future_focus.reliability_assessment: The findings are supported by a multicentre, longitudinal study (up to 7 years) with a robust sample size for primary analyses, utilizing multimodal data (genomics, MRI, NfL, cognition), and rigorous genomics and MRI processing pipelines. Linear mixed-effects models were used, accounting for presymptomatic/symptomatic status, relatedness, family structure, and population stratification. Serum NfL measurements were precise (mean intra-assay and inter-assay CV < 10%). The reliability is further supported by the robustness of ROI models against adjustments for population stratification and MRI scanner changes. However, neuropsychological assessments are considered less precise than imaging and biomarker measures. Limitations include insufficient sample size for secondary stratified analyses of rs1990622 AG and GG carriers, inconsistent memory tests across study phases, and a single test for the visuospatial domain, potentially reducing sensitivity. The absence of effects in non-carrier controls, contrasting with population-based studies, may be due to differences in study design and sample size.
recommended_alternatives: TMEM106B genotype assessment (as a modifying factor to be included in clinical trials, particularly for GRN- and C9orf72-related genetic FTD)
